tool.name: Redis
tool.tagline: In-memory data structure store for caching, queues, counters and real-time data
tool.description: Redis keeps data structures such as strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and streams in memory and serves them with sub-millisecond latency. It is the standard choice for caching, sessions, rate limiting, leaderboards, queues and pub/sub, and can persist to disk and replicate for availability.

glossary.def: The command-line program that comes with Redis: you type Redis commands into it and it shows the server's replies.
In Redis, a value made of named fields, each holding a string, all stored under one key, like one row of a table. (Elsewhere, a hash means a fingerprint computed from data.)
A Redis set in which every member has a number (its score), and members are kept in score order, which makes rankings and time-ordered lists fast.
The compact format Redis uses for small hashes, lists and sorted sets: items packed one after another, which saves a lot of memory.
The compact format Redis uses for a small set that holds only whole numbers.
In Redis's SCAN commands, the number returned with each batch that says where to continue; when it comes back as 0, the scan is finished.
In Redis, a value that is an append-only log: entries are only ever added at the end, each with a time-based ID, and readers can go back over them.
A named group of readers of a Redis stream that share its entries out, so each entry goes to just one of them, and that tracks which entries are done.
One reader in a Redis consumer group, usually a worker program, that receives entries from a stream and confirms each one when done.
For a Redis consumer group, the list of stream entries handed to a consumer but not yet confirmed with XACK.
A caching pattern: the app asks the cache first, and on a miss loads the data from the database and stores a copy in the cache for next time.
A popular cached value expires and many requests miss at the same moment, all hitting the database at once.
Caching the fact that something was not found, for a short time, so repeated lookups of a missing item don't keep reaching the database.
A caching pattern where every write goes to the cache and the database together, so the cache is always up to date.
A caching pattern where writes go to the cache first and are saved to the database later, which is fast but can lose data if the cache fails.
A small random amount added to a time, such as an expiry or a wait before trying again, so that many things don't happen in the same instant.
A cap on how often someone may do something, such as 5 login attempts per minute; extra attempts are refused until the limit resets.
A rate-limiting method that counts actions per calendar slot, such as per minute, and resets the count when a new slot starts.
A rate-limiting method that records the time of every action and counts those within the last N seconds, so there are no bursts at slot edges.
A rate-limiting method that estimates the last N seconds by blending the counts of the current and previous fixed slots; cheaper than a full log.
A rate-limiting method: each user has an allowance that refills at a steady rate up to a maximum, and each action spends one unit.
In Redis, sending many commands without waiting for each reply and reading all the replies afterwards, which saves network round trips.
Not blocking anyone while you work, but checking at the end whether someone else changed the data meanwhile, and trying again if they did.
Writing a new value only if the data is still what you last read; otherwise the write is refused and you try again.
Sending a message without storing it or waiting for confirmation: whoever is listening gets it, anyone else misses it for good.
A Redis Cluster version of Pub/Sub where each channel lives on one server instead of being copied to all of them.
A Redis feature that announces events about keys, such as a key expiring, as Pub/Sub messages.
A Redis string used as a long row of 0/1 values, one per position, for cheap per-id yes/no flags and counts.
A Redis structure that estimates how many distinct items it has seen, within about 1%, using at most 12 KB whatever the count.
A small programming language that Redis can run on the server, so a script of several commands runs as one atomic step.
Named Lua functions loaded into Redis once and called with FCALL; unlike plain scripts they are saved with the data and copied to replicas.
Redis Database file: a compact snapshot of all Redis data at one moment, written to disk at intervals.
Append-only file: a Redis file that records every write command, so the data can be rebuilt after a restart.
Making a copy of a running program; Redis forks so the copy can save data to disk while the original keeps serving clients.
Forcing data that a program has written all the way onto the disk, instead of letting the operating system keep it in memory for a while.
The Redis setting that decides what to delete, or whether to refuse writes, when memory is full.
Removing data from a full cache or memory to make room for new data.
Least recently used: when room is needed, remove the item that hasn't been used for the longest time.
Least frequently used: when room is needed, remove the item used the fewest times.
A Redis key holding a huge value, such as a list or hash with millions of items, which uses lots of memory and makes the server pause when deleted or moved.
In Redis replication, the server that accepts writes and sends them on to its replicas.
A Redis replica catching up after a short disconnect by replaying only the writes it missed, instead of copying all the data again.
A fixed-size buffer of recent writes kept by a Redis primary so that replicas that briefly disconnect can catch up.
A Redis program, run as three or more copies, that watches a primary and automatically promotes a replica if the primary fails.
Two servers both acting as the primary at the same time, usually after a network break, so writes to one of them get lost.
Redis's built-in way of spreading data over several primaries (each with replicas) by giving each one a share of the 16384 hash slots.
One of the 16384 numbered buckets of Redis Cluster; every key belongs to one slot, and each primary server owns some of the slots.
The part of a Redis key inside {curly braces}; only it decides the key's slot, so keys with the same tag land on the same server.
An extra Redis thread that only reads incoming commands and sends replies over the network; commands still run on the main thread.

concepts.name: What Redis is and redis-cli
concepts.summary: Redis is a database server that keeps all its data in memory and stores values as ready-made structures such as lists and sets.
concepts.why: Knowing how Redis works (data in memory, one command at a time, typed values) explains every design choice that follows.
concepts.body:
A relational database keeps its tables on disk and answers any SQL query. **Redis** makes a different trade: it keeps all its data in the computer's **memory** (**RAM**), the fast working storage programs use while they run. Reading from memory takes microseconds, far quicker than disk.

Redis has no tables. It is a **key-value store**: every piece of data is a value stored under a name, its **key**, like a coat check: each coat (the value) hangs under a ticket number (the key), and you get the coat back by showing the ticket.

Unlike a plain key-value store, the values have types. A value can be a string, but also a list, a set, a sorted set and more, which the next lessons cover. You change them with short commands such as `SET`, `LPUSH` or `ZADD`, and the server does the work for you.

Redis runs commands **one at a time**, in order. So every single command is **atomic**: no other client's command can run halfway through yours. Two users adding 1 to the same counter at once always get both additions counted.

Redis can also save its data to disk and copy it to other servers, but it is designed for data that fits in memory. It is usually used next to a main database, not instead of one: as a **cache** (a fast copy of data that is slow to fetch or compute), for counters, job lists and the like.

You talk to Redis from a **terminal** (the text window where you type commands) with **redis-cli**, the Redis command-line client. Run it on its own and type commands one by one, or put a single command after it: `redis-cli SET greeting hello`. Useful basics:

- `PING` replies `PONG`; `SELECT 1` switches to database number 1 (a Redis server has 16 numbered databases, 0 by default),
- `KEYS *` lists every key, but freezes the server while it works through a big database; `SCAN` (two lessons on) is the safe way,
- `TYPE key` tells you the type of a value, and `FLUSHDB` deletes everything in the current database.

Key names can be any text. The convention is to build them from parts separated by colons, like `user:42:profile`, so related keys share a prefix, much like folders.
concepts.code:
redis-cli PING                          # PONG
redis-cli SET user:42:name "Ana"        # OK
redis-cli GET user:42:name              # "Ana"
redis-cli TYPE user:42:name             # string
redis-cli EXISTS user:42:name user:7    # (integer) 1
redis-cli DBSIZE                        # (integer) 1
redis-cli GET missing                   # (nil)
takeaways: Keys map to typed values, all held in memory
Each command is atomic; commands run one at a time
Use structured key names like user:42:profile
Avoid KEYS * on a live server; it freezes it
pitfalls: Running KEYS * on a busy server with millions of keys and making every client wait.

quiz.q: Two clients run INCR counter at the same moment. Why is the final value always correct?
options: It isn't; one increment can be lost
Commands execute one at a time, so each INCR is atomic
quiz.explain: Redis executes commands one after another, so a single command never mixes with another.

concepts.name: Strings and counters
concepts.summary: Store text, numbers or any other data in string values, read them back, and count safely with INCR.
concepts.why: Strings are the most used type: cached values, on/off flags, one-time codes and counters.
concepts.body:
A Redis **string** is the simplest kind of value: a sequence of bytes up to 512 MB (**megabytes**, about 512 million bytes). Usually it's text or a number, but it can hold any data, even an image. `SET key value` writes it and `GET key` reads it.

`MGET` and `MSET` read or write several keys in one command. That matters because every command is a message to the server and a reply back (a **round trip**), and each one takes time.

`SET` has options that make it far more than a plain write:

- `EX 60` or `PX 60000` makes the key expire after 60 seconds (or 60,000 milliseconds),
- `NX` only sets the key if it does not exist yet, `XX` only if it does,
- `GET` returns the old value while setting the new one.

`SET lock:report me NX EX 30` sets a key only if nobody else has, for 30 seconds. Because only one client can succeed, it works as a simple **lock**: whoever set the key may run the report, and the lock frees itself if they crash.

If a string holds a whole number, `INCR`, `INCRBY`, `DECR` and `INCRBYFLOAT` change it and return the new value; a missing key counts as 0. Each is a single atomic command, so counters (page views, login attempts per minute, the next order number) never miss a count, even with many clients. `APPEND`, `STRLEN`, `GETRANGE` and `SETRANGE` work directly on the stored bytes.

Some apps store a whole record in one string, written as **JSON**, a common text format for structured data such as `{"user": 42, "plan": "pro"}`. That's fine when you always read and write the whole thing. When you need to change one part, a hash (next lessons) is a better fit.
concepts.code:
redis-cli SET page:home:views 0          # OK
redis-cli INCR page:home:views           # (integer) 1
redis-cli INCRBY page:home:views 10      # (integer) 11
redis-cli SET session:abc '{"user":42}' EX 3600   # OK
redis-cli TTL session:abc                # (integer) 3600
redis-cli SET lock:job1 worker-a NX EX 30   # OK
redis-cli SET lock:job1 worker-b NX EX 30   # (nil)  already held
redis-cli MGET page:home:views lock:job1    # 1) "11"  2) "worker-a"
redis-cli INCR session:abc
# (error) ERR value is not an integer or out of range
takeaways: Strings hold any bytes up to 512 MB
SET supports EX/PX expiry and NX/XX conditions
INCR and friends are atomic counters; missing keys start at 0
MGET/MSET handle several keys in one round trip
pitfalls: Reading the value, adding 1 in your own code and writing it back instead of using INCR: two clients doing that at once lose an update.

quiz.q: What does SET k v NX return when k already exists?
quiz.explain: NX only sets a missing key; otherwise the reply is nil and nothing changes.

concepts.name: Keys, expiry and SCAN
concepts.summary: Delete keys, make them expire with EXPIRE and TTL, and go through all keys safely with SCAN.
concepts.why: Making data expire on its own is what makes Redis a good cache, and listing keys safely keeps a live server responsive.
concepts.body:
Any key can have a **time to live** (**TTL**): a number of seconds after which Redis deletes it by itself. `EXPIRE key 60` sets it in seconds (`PEXPIRE` for milliseconds, `EXPIREAT` for an exact moment given as a **Unix timestamp**, the number of seconds since 1 January 1970). `TTL key` reports the seconds left and `PERSIST key` removes the expiry. `TTL` returns -1 for a key without expiry and -2 for a key that doesn't exist.

Expiry details that bite:

- overwriting a key with `SET` (without `KEEPTTL`) clears its TTL,
- commands that change a value in place, such as `INCR`, `LPUSH` or `HSET`, keep it,
- expired keys are deleted when someone next touches them and by a regular background check, so memory is freed gradually; but an expired key is never returned.

Deleting: `DEL key ...` frees the memory at once, which can make the server pause for a moment on a huge value; `UNLINK` returns immediately and frees the memory in the background. `RENAME` gives a key a new name.

To find keys, never use `KEYS pattern` on a live server: it goes through every key in one go, and no other command runs until it finishes. `SCAN cursor MATCH pattern COUNT n` returns a small batch of keys plus a **cursor**, a bookmark saying where to continue. You call `SCAN` again with that cursor until it comes back as 0.

`SCAN` may return a key more than once, and keys added or removed during the scan may be missed, so make your processing safe to repeat. `HSCAN`, `SSCAN` and `ZSCAN` go through the items inside big hashes, sets and sorted sets the same way.

Good key names (`app:entity:id:field`) make `SCAN MATCH` and tracking down problems much easier.
concepts.code:
redis-cli SET otp:ana 123456 EX 300     # OK
redis-cli TTL otp:ana                   # (integer) 300
redis-cli SET otp:ana 654321            # OK  (plain SET clears the TTL)
redis-cli TTL otp:ana                   # (integer) -1
redis-cli EXPIRE otp:ana 120            # (integer) 1
redis-cli TTL nothing-here              # (integer) -2

redis-cli MSET user:1 a user:2 b order:1 c   # OK
redis-cli SCAN 0 MATCH 'user:*' COUNT 100
# 1) "0"            next cursor (0 = finished)
# 2) 1) "user:1"
#    2) "user:2"
redis-cli --scan --pattern 'user:*'     # redis-cli repeats SCAN for you
redis-cli UNLINK user:1 user:2          # (integer) 2
takeaways: EXPIRE/TTL manage time to live; -1 = no TTL, -2 = no key
A plain SET resets the TTL; in-place updates keep it
Use SCAN (or redis-cli --scan), never KEYS, on live servers
UNLINK frees big values without making the server pause
pitfalls: Refreshing a cached value with SET and forgetting to pass EX again, so it never expires.

quiz.q: A key has TTL 100. You run SET on it without options. What is its TTL now?
quiz.explain: SET replaces the value and discards the old TTL unless KEEPTTL is given.

concepts.name: Hashes
concepts.summary: Store a record as a hash of named fields and read or update single fields with HSET, HGET and HINCRBY.
concepts.why: Hashes are the natural way to keep records like users or shopping carts while updating fields independently.
concepts.body:
A **hash** is one key holding a set of named **fields**, each with a string value, much like one row of a table: `HSET user:42 name Ana plan pro logins 0` stores three fields under the key `user:42`.

- `HGET key field` and `HMGET key f1 f2` read fields, `HGETALL key` reads all of them,
- `HSET` creates or updates one or more fields and returns how many were new,
- `HINCRBY key field n` adds to one number field atomically,
- `HDEL`, `HEXISTS`, `HLEN`, `HKEYS`, `HVALS` do what they say, and `HSETNX` sets a field only if it is absent.

Compared with storing the whole record as one JSON string, a hash lets you change one field without reading and rewriting everything, and two clients updating different fields at the same time don't overwrite each other. Values are flat strings, though: a field can't contain another hash or a list. For nested data use several keys, or the JSON data type built into Redis 8.

Small hashes are stored in a compact format called **listpack**, so many small hashes take much less memory than the same data spread over many separate string keys.

Expiry normally applies to the whole key. Since Redis 7.4 you can also expire single fields with `HEXPIRE`, handy when each field is a separately cached value.

`HGETALL` on a hash with hundreds of thousands of fields is slow and holds up every other client. Go through big hashes in small batches with `HSCAN`, or keep them small.
concepts.code:
redis-cli HSET user:42 name Ana plan pro logins 0   # (integer) 3
redis-cli HGET user:42 plan                        # "pro"
redis-cli HINCRBY user:42 logins 1                 # (integer) 1
redis-cli HSET user:42 plan team                   # (integer) 0  (updated, not new)
redis-cli HMGET user:42 name plan email
# 1) "Ana"
# 2) "team"
# 3) (nil)
redis-cli HGETALL user:42
# 1) "name"  2) "Ana"  3) "plan"  4) "team"  5) "logins"  6) "1"
redis-cli HDEL user:42 logins                      # (integer) 1
redis-cli HLEN user:42                             # (integer) 2
takeaways: A hash is a flat set of field -> string pairs under one key
Update one field with HSET or HINCRBY without touching the others
Small hashes use a compact format and save memory
Expiry is per key; HEXPIRE (7.4+) expires single fields
pitfalls: Calling HGETALL on huge hashes in code that runs on every page view.

quiz.q: Why prefer a hash over a JSON string when two programs update different fields of the same user at the same time?
options: Each HSET touches only its field, so updates don't overwrite each other
JSON strings can't be stored in Redis
quiz.explain: Reading, changing and rewriting a whole JSON string loses changes made at the same time; per-field updates don't.

concepts.name: Lists and simple queues
concepts.summary: Use lists as queues, stacks and capped feeds with LPUSH, RPOP, LRANGE, LTRIM and pops that wait for data.
concepts.why: Lists power job queues, recent-activity feeds and capped histories, with fast adds and removals at both ends.
concepts.body:
A **list** is an ordered sequence of strings, fast to change at both ends. `LPUSH`/`RPUSH` add to the left/right, `LPOP`/`RPOP` remove (optionally several at once), `LLEN` gives the length and `LRANGE key 0 -1` reads a range by position, counting from 0 (negative positions count from the end).

Pick the ends to get the behaviour you want:

- **queue** (first in, first out, like a line at a shop counter): `LPUSH` to add, `RPOP` to take,
- **stack** (last in, first out, like a pile of plates): `LPUSH` and `LPOP`,
- **capped list**: `LPUSH` then `LTRIM key 0 99` keeps only the newest 100 items, perfect for "recent activity".

A common use is a job queue: your app pushes jobs ("send this email") and separate **worker** programs take them off and do them. A worker shouldn't keep asking "anything yet?" over and over. `BRPOP queue 5` waits until an item arrives or 5 seconds pass (0 = wait forever), and can watch several lists at once, preferring them in the order given.

Popping removes the item, so a worker that crashes right after `BRPOP` loses the job. `LMOVE source processing RIGHT LEFT` (and its waiting form `BLMOVE`) moves the item to a second "processing" list in one atomic step. The worker removes it from there when done, and jobs left behind by a crash can be put back. When every job must be done, with confirmations, Redis streams (an Advanced lesson) are the better tool.

Reading or changing an item in the middle (`LINDEX`, `LSET`, `LREM`) has to walk along the list, so it gets slower the longer the list is. Lists are for the ends and the ranges near them, not for jumping to any position.
concepts.code:
redis-cli RPUSH jobs email:1 email:2 email:3    # (integer) 3
redis-cli LPOP jobs                             # "email:1"  (FIFO with RPUSH + LPOP)
redis-cli LMOVE jobs jobs:processing LEFT RIGHT # "email:2"  safe hand-off
redis-cli LRANGE jobs:processing 0 -1           # 1) "email:2"
redis-cli LREM jobs:processing 1 email:2        # (integer) 1  done, remove it

# capped feed of the 3 newest events
redis-cli LPUSH feed:42 a b c d e               # (integer) 5
redis-cli LTRIM feed:42 0 2                     # OK
redis-cli LRANGE feed:42 0 -1                   # 1) "e"  2) "d"  3) "c"

redis-cli BRPOP empty-queue 1                   # (nil) after waiting 1 second
takeaways: LPUSH/RPUSH and LPOP/RPOP are fast at either end, whatever the length
LPUSH + LTRIM keeps a capped list of the newest items
BRPOP/BLMOVE let workers wait for jobs instead of asking repeatedly
LMOVE to a processing list avoids losing jobs on crashes
pitfalls: Using LINDEX or LREM on long lists in code that runs constantly: they get slower as the list grows.

quiz.q: You LPUSH events and want only the newest 50. Which command keeps them?
quiz.explain: LPUSH puts the newest at index 0, so keep indexes 0 to 49.

concepts.name: Sets
concepts.summary: Store unique unordered members with SADD and test membership, intersect and union sets on the server.
concepts.why: Sets answer 'have we seen this?', 'who is online?' and 'what do these groups share?' in one command.
concepts.body:
A **set** is an unordered collection of unique strings, like a party's guest list: each name appears once, in no particular order. `SADD key m1 m2` adds members and returns how many were new, so adding a duplicate does nothing. `SISMEMBER key m` (or `SMISMEMBER` for several) checks membership instantly however big the set is, `SREM` removes, `SCARD` counts and `SMEMBERS` returns everything.

Comparing sets on the server is the standout feature:

- `SINTER a b` members in both, `SUNION a b` in either, `SDIFF a b` in a but not b,
- `SINTERSTORE dest a b` saves the result as a new set, and `SINTERCARD` just counts it.

That makes queries like "tags shared by two articles" or "friends of Ana who are online" one round trip with no data shipped to the app.

`SRANDMEMBER key n` samples members without removing them; `SPOP` removes and returns random ones, handy for lotteries or distributing work.

Typical uses: unique visitors per day (`SADD visitors:2026-10-17 user42`), tags, permissions, de-duplication of jobs, and online-user tracking.

`SMEMBERS` and large `SINTER` calls take longer the bigger the sets are; on sets with millions of members, go through them in batches with `SSCAN`. When you only need a rough count of unique items, a HyperLogLog (a Practical lesson) uses a few **kilobytes** (thousands of bytes) instead of memory that grows with every member.
concepts.code:
redis-cli SADD online ana ben cy            # (integer) 3
redis-cli SADD online ana                   # (integer) 0  already a member
redis-cli SISMEMBER online ben              # (integer) 1
redis-cli SADD friends:ana ben di cy        # (integer) 3
redis-cli SINTER online friends:ana         # 1) "ben" 2) "cy"  (order not guaranteed)
redis-cli SDIFF friends:ana online          # 1) "di"
redis-cli SCARD online                      # (integer) 3
redis-cli SREM online cy                    # (integer) 1
takeaways: Sets hold unique members; SADD ignores duplicates
SISMEMBER answers instantly, whatever the set's size
SINTER, SUNION, SDIFF compute on the server
Members are unordered; use a sorted set when order matters
pitfalls: Relying on SMEMBERS returning members in insertion order.

quiz.q: Which command returns the members of friends:ana who are also in online?
quiz.explain: SINTER returns members present in all given sets.

concepts.name: Sorted sets and leaderboards
concepts.summary: Keep members ordered by a numeric score with ZADD and query by rank or score range for leaderboards and timelines.
concepts.why: Sorted sets make leaderboards, most-urgent-first job lists and time-ordered lookups simple and fast.
concepts.body:
A **sorted set** (also called a zset) is a set where every unique member has a number, its **score**, and members are kept in score order (ties are ordered alphabetically by member). Adding, updating and finding a member stay fast even with millions of members.

- `ZADD key score member` adds or updates; `ZINCRBY key 10 ana` adds to a score,
- `ZRANGE key 0 9 REV WITHSCORES` gives the top 10 (highest first),
- `ZRANK`/`ZREVRANK` give a member's position, `ZSCORE` its score,
- `ZRANGE key 100 200 BYSCORE` returns members with scores from 100 to 200, both included. A `(` in front of a number leaves that number out: `(120` means "more than 120", not 120 itself. `-inf` and `+inf` (minus and plus infinity) mean "no lower limit" and "no upper limit",
- `ZREM`, `ZCARD`, `ZCOUNT key min max`, and `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` to trim.

`ZADD` flags refine updates: `NX` only adds new members, `XX` only updates existing ones, `GT`/`LT` only update when the new score is greater/less, perfect for "best score" tables.

Using timestamps as scores turns a zset into a time index: "events in the last hour" is `ZRANGE key <cutoff> +inf BYSCORE`, where the cutoff is the current time minus 3600 seconds, and trimming old entries is `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key -inf cutoff`. `ZPOPMIN` and its waiting form `BZPOPMIN` take the member with the lowest score, which gives a job list where the most urgent (lowest score) goes first.
concepts.code:
redis-cli ZADD game:lb 120 ana 95 ben 150 cy     # (integer) 3
redis-cli ZINCRBY game:lb 40 ben                 # "135"
redis-cli ZRANGE game:lb 0 1 REV WITHSCORES
# 1) "cy"  2) "150"  3) "ben"  4) "135"
redis-cli ZREVRANK game:lb ana                   # (integer) 2   (0-based)
redis-cli ZADD game:lb GT 100 cy                 # (integer) 0   lower score ignored
redis-cli ZSCORE game:lb cy                      # "150"
redis-cli ZRANGE game:lb 100 140 BYSCORE         # 1) "ana" 2) "ben"
redis-cli ZCOUNT game:lb '(120' +inf             # (integer) 2   more than 120, no upper limit
takeaways: Members are unique and ordered by score; operations stay fast at any size
ZRANGE ... REV WITHSCORES for top-N; ZREVRANK for a member's rank
BYSCORE picks a score range; (120 leaves 120 out, and -inf/+inf mean no limit
Timestamps as scores make a time-ordered index
pitfalls: Expecting ZRANK to be 1-based: ranks start at 0.

quiz.q: Which ZADD flag updates a player's score only if the new score is higher?
quiz.explain: GT updates existing members only when the new score is greater (and still adds new members).

quiz.q: Scores are timestamps. How do you fetch events from the last 60 seconds if now is 1000?
quiz.explain: BYSCORE selects by score range, here 940 to 1000.

concepts.name: Caching patterns
concepts.summary: Use cache-aside with TTLs, choose how to remove outdated entries, and protect the database when many requests miss at once.
concepts.why: Caching is the number one use of Redis, and naive caching serves out-of-date data or swamps the database.
concepts.body:
The common pattern is **cache-aside**: the app asks Redis first; on a **cache miss** (the key isn't there) it loads the data from the database, saves it in Redis with a TTL, and returns it. Nothing is cached until someone asks for it.

When data changes, the app writes to the database and then **deletes** the cache key rather than updating it, so the next read reloads fresh data. Removing outdated entries like this is called **cache invalidation**. Deleting is safer than setting: if two writers update the cache at about the same moment, their updates can arrive in the wrong order and leave an old value behind.

Design decisions:

- **Keys** include everything the value depends on: `cache:product:42:v3:hy` (product 42, data version 3, Armenian text).
- **TTL** limits how long an outdated value can live, even if a delete is missed. Add a little randomness (**jitter**) to TTLs so thousands of keys don't expire in the same second.
- **Format**: a JSON string when you always read the whole value, a hash when you read single fields.
- **Negative caching**: briefly cache "not found" too, so repeated lookups of a missing item don't keep hitting the database.

A **cache stampede** happens when a popular key expires and hundreds of **requests** (messages from users' browsers or apps asking for data) miss at once, all querying the database. Defences: a short lock with `SET lock:key token NX EX 5`, so only one request reloads the value while the others wait or use the old copy; refreshing popular keys a little before they expire; or keeping a backup copy with a longer TTL.

For a pure cache, set `maxmemory` and an eviction policy such as `allkeys-lru`, so when memory is full Redis deletes the least recently used keys instead of refusing writes (see the memory lesson).

Other patterns: **write-through** (write the cache and the database together) and **write-behind** (write the cache now, the database later), which trade simplicity for freshness or safety.
concepts.code:
# Cache-aside for product 42, step by step
redis-cli GET cache:product:42
# (nil)  cache miss: the app loads the product from the database, e.g.
#        SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE id = 42;
redis-cli SET lock:cache:product:42 1 NX EX 5
# OK     we hold the reload lock; other requests wait or use the database
redis-cli SET cache:product:42 '{"name":"Pen","price":1.5}' EX 337
# OK     cached for 300 seconds plus 37 seconds of random jitter
redis-cli DEL lock:cache:product:42      # (integer) 1  lock released
redis-cli GET cache:product:42
# "{\"name\":\"Pen\",\"price\":1.5}"  cache hit: no database query

# The product changes: update the database first...
#        UPDATE products SET price = 1.8 WHERE id = 42;
# ...then delete (don't overwrite) the cached copy
redis-cli DEL cache:product:42           # (integer) 1  next read reloads
takeaways: Cache-aside: read cache, on miss load the DB and SET with TTL
On writes, update the DB then delete the cache key
Add TTL jitter and a recompute lock to avoid stampedes
For pure caches, set maxmemory with an allkeys eviction policy
pitfalls: Caching without a TTL and relying only on deletes: one missed delete serves outdated data forever.

quiz.q: Why do most cache-aside implementations delete the cache key after a write instead of setting the new value?
options: Concurrent writers setting the cache can leave an older value last; deleting forces a fresh reload
Deleted keys use less memory permanently
quiz.explain: Delete-on-write avoids ordering races between concurrent cache updates.

concepts.name: Rate limiting with counters
concepts.summary: Limit how often each user can do something with fixed-window and sliding-window counters built from INCR, EXPIRE and sorted sets.
concepts.why: Logins, password resets, text messages and public web services all need limits per user, and Redis is the usual shared place to count.
concepts.body:
A **rate limit** caps how often someone may do something, such as 5 login attempts per minute. The simplest version is a **fixed window**: count each user's requests (attempts) per minute. The key includes the minute number, e.g. `rl:ana:` followed by the current Unix time divided by 60, rounded down. Each request runs `INCR key`, then `EXPIRE key 60`; if the count is over the limit, reject. Because `INCR` is atomic, attempts arriving at the same time from many app servers are all counted.

Send `INCR` and `EXPIRE` together in a transaction (`MULTI` ... `EXEC`, which has its own lesson), so a crash between them can't leave a counter that never expires. Setting the expiry on every request also works; it just stretches the window slightly.

Fixed windows allow bursts at the edges: a client could send the full limit at 12:00:59 and again at 12:01:00. A **sliding-window log** fixes this with a sorted set per client, scored by time:

- `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key -inf now-window` drops old entries,
- `ZADD key now unique-id` records this request,
- `ZCARD key` counts requests in the window,
- `EXPIRE key window` cleans up after idle clients.

A log costs memory for every request, so for high limits use a **sliding-window counter** (blend the counts of the current and previous fixed windows) or a **token bucket** (each user has an allowance that refills at a steady rate, and each request spends one unit), usually written as a Lua script (an Advanced lesson).

A web service usually answers a rejected request with the code `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` value saying when to try again. Limit by user account where possible, not only by network address, since many people can share one address.
concepts.code:
# Fixed window: 3 login attempts per minute for ana
# 29350000 is the current minute (Unix time 1761000000 divided by 60)
$ redis-cli
> MULTI
OK
> INCR rl:ana:29350000
QUEUED
> EXPIRE rl:ana:29350000 60
QUEUED
> EXEC
1) (integer) 1        # first attempt this minute: allowed
2) (integer) 1
# a 4th attempt in the same minute gets 4 from INCR: over the limit, reject

# Sliding-window log: one sorted-set entry per attempt, scored by time
> ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rls:ana -inf 1761000000      # drop attempts older than 60 s
(integer) 0
> ZADD rls:ana 1761000060 attempt-1761000060    # record this one (now = 1761000060)
(integer) 1
> ZCARD rls:ana                                  # attempts in the last 60 s
(integer) 1
> EXPIRE rls:ana 60                              # tidy up if ana goes quiet
(integer) 1
takeaways: Fixed window: INCR a per-window key and EXPIRE it
Send INCR and EXPIRE together so no counter lives forever
A sliding-window log is a sorted set of request times
Fixed windows allow bursts at the edges; sliding windows don't
pitfalls: Calling EXPIRE only when INCR returns 1, as a separate command: if that command fails, the key never expires and the user stays blocked forever.

quiz.q: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. What is the worst case a client can send within any 2 seconds?
quiz.explain: 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next.

concepts.name: Pipelining and clients
concepts.summary: Send many commands per network round trip with pipelining, and reuse connections from your app with a connection pool.
concepts.why: Waiting on the network, not Redis itself, is usually what makes many small commands slow; pipelining often makes them 10 times faster.
concepts.body:
Each command normally costs a full network **round trip**: send, wait, receive. At 0.5 ms per round trip, 10,000 `SET`s sent one after another take 5 seconds, even though Redis carries out each one in microseconds.

**Pipelining** sends many commands without waiting for each reply, then reads all the replies at once, like handing a shop assistant your whole list instead of asking for one item at a time. Every Redis **client library** (the ready-made code an app uses to talk to Redis, one for each programming language) supports it. Far more commands get done per second, because the server works through them back to back and the network carries a few big messages instead of thousands of tiny ones.

A pipeline is **not atomic** on its own: other clients' commands may run between yours. Some client libraries wrap a pipeline in `MULTI`/`EXEC` (a transaction, next lesson) by default; switch that off when you only want speed. Keep batches to a few thousand commands so the replies don't pile up in memory on either side.

Commands that take many keys or values at once (`MGET`, `MSET`, `HSET` with many fields, `SADD` with many members) are another way to save round trips.

Keeping connections healthy:

- open connections once and reuse them: a **connection pool** is a set of open connections an app keeps ready, because opening a new one for every command is slow,
- set time limits for connecting and for waiting on replies, so a dead server doesn't hang your app,
- to load a big file of commands from the terminal, use `redis-cli --pipe`.
concepts.code:
# redis-benchmark ships with Redis. 100,000 SETs, one command per round trip:
redis-benchmark -t set -n 100000 -q
# SET: 95238.10 requests per second        (example figure)

# the same, sending 16 commands per round trip (-P 16 = pipeline depth)
redis-benchmark -t set -n 100000 -q -P 16
# SET: 1030927.81 requests per second      (about 10 times faster)

# pipelining from the terminal: a file with one command per line
printf 'SET k:1 1\nSET k:2 2\nSET k:3 3\n' > cmds.txt
redis-cli --pipe < cmds.txt
# All data transferred. Waiting for the last reply...
# errors: 0, replies: 3
redis-cli MGET k:1 k:2 k:3                 # 1) "1"  2) "2"  3) "3"
takeaways: Round trips dominate the time; pipelines batch them
Pipelines are not atomic unless wrapped in MULTI/EXEC
Prefer commands that take many keys, like MGET, MSET, SADD with many members
Reuse pooled connections and set time limits
pitfalls: Opening a new connection for every command and paying the connection setup time every time.

quiz.q: Does a plain (non-transactional) pipeline guarantee no other client's command runs between yours?
options: No, other clients' commands can interleave
quiz.explain: Pipelining only saves network time; to keep others out you need MULTI/EXEC or a script.

concepts.name: MULTI/EXEC and WATCH
concepts.summary: Group commands to run atomically with MULTI/EXEC and use WATCH for optimistic check-and-set.
concepts.why: Some updates span several keys or depend on a value you read, and must not mix with other clients' commands.
concepts.body:
`MULTI` starts a transaction. The commands you send after it are **queued**, put in a waiting line (the server replies `QUEUED`), and `EXEC` runs them all back to back with no other client's commands in between. `DISCARD` throws the queue away.

Redis transactions are different from SQL ones:

- there is **no rollback**: if a command fails while running (say `INCR` on a value that isn't a number), the others still take effect,
- a mistyped command, caught while queuing, makes `EXEC` cancel the whole transaction,
- you can't read a value and decide based on it inside `MULTI`, because replies only arrive at `EXEC`.

For check-then-act logic use **optimistic locking** with `WATCH`: instead of blocking other clients, you go ahead and let Redis tell you if someone got in first. `WATCH key` before `MULTI`; read the values you need; queue the writes; call `EXEC`. If any watched key changed in the meantime, `EXEC` returns nil and nothing runs, so you try again. This is called **check-and-set** (CAS).

Client libraries offer helpers that do the watch, check and try-again steps for you.

For complex logic, or when other clients change the watched key so often that you keep trying again, a Lua script (an Advanced lesson) is usually simpler and faster: Redis runs it on the server as one atomic step, and it can read and write in one go.
concepts.code:
$ redis-cli
> SET stock:pen 3        # OK
> WATCH stock:pen          # tell me if anyone changes this key
OK
> GET stock:pen            # check: 3 left, so we may sell one
"3"
> MULTI
OK
> DECR stock:pen
QUEUED
> RPUSH orders pen
QUEUED
> EXEC                     # would be (nil) if stock:pen had changed
1) (integer) 2
2) (integer) 1

> MULTI
OK
> SET a x                  # replies QUEUED, as do the next two
> INCR a
> SET b y
> EXEC
1) OK
2) (error) ERR value is not an integer or out of range
3) OK                      # no rollback: both SETs took effect
takeaways: MULTI queues, EXEC runs the queue atomically
No rollback: a failing command doesn't undo the others
WATCH + EXEC gives optimistic check-and-set; nil means try again
Use Lua when logic must read and decide atomically
pitfalls: Expecting a failed command inside EXEC to roll back the rest.

quiz.q: Inside MULTI, the second of three commands fails while running with WRONGTYPE (wrong kind of value). What happens?
options: The first and third commands still take effect
quiz.explain: Redis transactions have no rollback; only the failing command errors.

quiz.q: You WATCH balance, read it, then MULTI ... EXEC, but another client changed balance in between. What does EXEC do?
quiz.explain: A modified watched key aborts the transaction so you can retry.

concepts.name: Pub/Sub messaging
concepts.summary: Broadcast messages to everyone listening on a channel with PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE, knowing that missed messages are gone.
concepts.why: Pub/Sub is the simplest way to push live events, such as chat messages or 'this data changed' signals, to many running programs at once.
concepts.body:
**Pub/Sub** (publish/subscribe) works like a radio station: senders broadcast on a named channel, and whoever is tuned in at that moment hears it. Senders and receivers don't need to know about each other. Receivers run `SUBSCRIBE news` (or `PSUBSCRIBE news.*` to match channel names by pattern, where `*` means anything), and their connection then just listens. Senders run `PUBLISH news "hello"`, which returns how many subscribers received it.

Delivery is **fire-and-forget**: each message is delivered at most once.

- messages are not stored; a subscriber that is offline or reconnecting misses them,
- there is no confirmation of receipt and no replay,
- a subscriber that reads too slowly, so that unsent messages pile up past a limit, is disconnected.

That's fine for short-lived signals: "user is typing" indicators, live dashboards, telling every app server to forget a cached value, or passing chat messages between the servers that hold users' live connections. When messages must be kept, replayed or shared out as jobs, use Redis streams (an Advanced lesson).

Usually a subscribed connection can only run subscription commands, so **client libraries** (the code apps use to talk to Redis) open a separate connection for subscribing. Channel names are shared by all the numbered databases.

In a Redis Cluster (several Redis servers sharing the data, an Expert lesson), a classic `PUBLISH` is copied to every server. **Sharded Pub/Sub** (`SSUBSCRIBE`/`SPUBLISH`, Redis 7.0+) keeps each channel on one server, which scales much better.

Keyspace notifications (`notify-keyspace-events`) use Pub/Sub to announce events such as a key expiring, so they have the same fire-and-forget delivery.
concepts.code:
# terminal 1: listen on a channel
redis-cli SUBSCRIBE news
# 1) "subscribe"  2) "news"  3) (integer) 1      ...and waits

# terminal 2: publish
redis-cli PUBLISH news "hello"            # (integer) 1  one subscriber got it
redis-cli PUBLISH nobody-listens "lost"   # (integer) 0  the message is gone
# terminal 1 now shows: 1) "message"  2) "news"  3) "hello"

# terminal 3: subscribe to every channel whose name starts with alerts.
redis-cli PSUBSCRIBE 'alerts.*'
# terminal 2:
redis-cli PUBLISH alerts.disk "90% full"  # (integer) 1  matched by the pattern
# terminal 3 shows: 1) "pmessage" 2) "alerts.*" 3) "alerts.disk" 4) "90% full"
takeaways: SUBSCRIBE/PSUBSCRIBE receive, PUBLISH sends and returns the receiver count
Missed messages are gone: no storage, no replay, no confirmations
Use a separate connection for subscribing
In Redis Cluster prefer sharded Pub/Sub (SPUBLISH/SSUBSCRIBE)
pitfalls: Using Pub/Sub to hand out jobs: jobs published while the programs doing them restart are simply lost.

quiz.q: A subscriber program restarts for 3 seconds while messages are published on its channel. What happens to those messages?
options: They are lost for that worker
They are queued until it reconnects
quiz.explain: Pub/Sub keeps no history; disconnected subscribers miss messages.

concepts.name: Bitmaps and HyperLogLog
concepts.summary: Count and flag huge numbers of items in very little memory with bitmaps (SETBIT, BITCOUNT) and HyperLogLog (PFADD, PFCOUNT).
concepts.why: Daily active users, on/off flags per user and unique counts over millions of ids are cheap with the right structure.
concepts.body:
A bit is the smallest unit of data, a single 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits. **Bitmaps** aren't a separate type: they are string values you read and write one bit at a time. `SETBIT key offset 1` sets the bit at position `offset`, `GETBIT` reads it, `BITCOUNT` counts the bits set to 1, and `BITOP AND|OR|XOR|NOT dest k1 k2` combines bitmaps bit by bit.

With whole-number user ids as positions, one bitmap per day records who was active: 10 million users take about 1.2 MB. "Active on both days" is a `BITOP AND` followed by `BITCOUNT`. (`BITFIELD` packs small numbers into a string the same way.)

Bitmaps waste space if ids are huge or far apart, because the string grows to reach the highest position.

**HyperLogLog** (HLL) estimates how many **distinct** items you've added. `PFADD key item ...` adds, `PFCOUNT key` returns the estimate, usually within about 1% (the typical error is 0.81%), and `PFMERGE` combines several, for example seven daily HLLs into a weekly unique count. Each HLL uses at most 12 KB however many items you add. You can't list or remove items; it only counts.

Choose by question:

- exact yes/no per id, with whole-number ids without big gaps: bitmap,
- rough unique count of any strings: HyperLogLog,
- exact unique count where memory is no problem: set.

Redis 8 also ships Bloom filters, Cuckoo filters, Count-min sketch and Top-K for other approximate questions, such as "have I probably seen this before?"
concepts.code:
redis-cli SETBIT active:2026-10-16 42 1      # (integer) 0  (previous bit value)
redis-cli SETBIT active:2026-10-16 7 1       # (integer) 0
redis-cli SETBIT active:2026-10-17 42 1      # (integer) 0
redis-cli BITCOUNT active:2026-10-16         # (integer) 2
redis-cli BITOP AND both active:2026-10-16 active:2026-10-17   # (integer) 6 (bytes)
redis-cli BITCOUNT both                      # (integer) 1   user 42 on both days
redis-cli GETBIT active:2026-10-17 7         # (integer) 0

redis-cli PFADD visitors:mon ana ben cy      # (integer) 1
redis-cli PFADD visitors:tue ben di          # (integer) 1
redis-cli PFMERGE visitors:week visitors:mon visitors:tue   # OK
redis-cli PFCOUNT visitors:week              # (integer) 4
takeaways: Bitmaps: one bit per integer id, combine with BITOP, count with BITCOUNT
HyperLogLog: unique counts within about 1% in at most 12 KB
PFMERGE turns daily HLLs into weekly or monthly counts
Sets for exact counts, HLL when approximate is fine
pitfalls: Using a bitmap with very large or scattered ids (like a random 18-digit number) and creating a gigantic string.

quiz.q: You need the approximate number of distinct search queries per day, possibly hundreds of millions. Which structure?
quiz.explain: HyperLogLog counts distinct strings in fixed small memory with under 1% error.

concepts.name: Streams and consumer groups
concepts.summary: Append events to a stream with XADD and handle them reliably with consumer groups, acknowledgements and claiming.
concepts.why: Streams give Redis messaging that is kept, can be replayed and reaches every entry at least once, for event processing and job queues.
concepts.body:
A **stream** is an append-only log: a list of entries you only ever add to the end of, like a ship's logbook. `XADD orders * item pen qty 2` appends an entry whose ID (`*` = auto) is `<milliseconds>-<sequence>`, so entries are time-ordered. `XRANGE key - +` reads a range, `XREAD BLOCK 5000 STREAMS key $` waits for new entries, and `XLEN` counts them. Unlike Pub/Sub, entries stay until you trim them, so readers can go back over history.

**Consumer groups** share entries out among workers, each of which is a **consumer** of the group:

- `XGROUP CREATE orders billing $ MKSTREAM` creates a group starting at new entries (`0` to start from the oldest entry),
- each worker calls `XREADGROUP GROUP billing worker-1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS orders >`; `>` means entries never delivered to this group, and each entry goes to only one consumer in the group,
- delivered entries sit in the group's **pending entries list** (PEL) until the worker confirms it's done with `XACK` (an acknowledgement).

If a worker crashes, its entries stay pending. Other workers find them with `XPENDING` and take them over with `XAUTOCLAIM` once they've sat untouched for a set time. Together this gives **at-least-once delivery**: every entry gets handled, but some may be handled twice, so make handling an entry twice harmless (**idempotent**: doing it twice has the same effect as once).

Several groups can read the same stream independently, like separate subscriptions. Cap growth with `XADD key MAXLEN ~ 100000 * ...` or `XTRIM`; the `~` allows efficient approximate trimming. Never trim entries that are still pending if you need them.
concepts.code:
redis-cli XGROUP CREATE orders billing '$' MKSTREAM       # OK
redis-cli XADD orders '*' item pen qty 2                  # "1760700000000-0"
redis-cli XADD orders '*' item pad qty 1                  # "1760700000001-0"

redis-cli XREADGROUP GROUP billing w1 COUNT 1 STREAMS orders '>'
# 1) 1) "orders"
#    2) 1) 1) "1760700000000-0"
#          2) 1) "item" 2) "pen" 3) "qty" 4) "2"
redis-cli XPENDING orders billing                         # 1 pending, owned by w1
redis-cli XACK orders billing 1760700000000-0             # (integer) 1

# w1 died holding an entry? another worker claims entries idle > 60 s
redis-cli XAUTOCLAIM orders billing w2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10
redis-cli XADD orders MAXLEN '~' 100000 '*' item ink qty 5   # append and trim
takeaways: XADD appends entries with time-based IDs; entries stay until trimmed
Consumer groups split entries among consumers; > reads new entries
Entries stay pending until XACK; XAUTOCLAIM recovers from crashed workers
Delivery is at-least-once: make handlers idempotent
pitfalls: Never calling XACK: the pending list grows forever and keeps using more memory.
Letting a stream grow unbounded without MAXLEN or XTRIM.

quiz.q: A consumer reads an entry with XREADGROUP ... > and crashes before XACK. What happens to the entry?
options: It is deleted from the stream
It is redelivered automatically to all consumers
It stays in the pending list and can be claimed by another consumer
quiz.explain: Unacknowledged entries remain pending and can be taken over with XCLAIM/XAUTOCLAIM.

concepts.name: Lua scripts and functions
concepts.summary: Run logic atomically on the server with EVAL and Redis Functions, passing keys and arguments correctly.
concepts.why: A script turns a read, decide, write sequence into one atomic operation with a single round trip.
concepts.body:
Sometimes you need to read a value, decide, and write, without anyone else getting in between. `EVAL script numkeys key... arg...` sends a small program, a **script** written in the **Lua** language, for Redis to run on the server. Inside, `KEYS[1]` and `ARGV[1]` hold the inputs and `redis.call("GET", KEYS[1])` runs commands (`redis.pcall` returns errors instead of stopping the script).

The whole script is **atomic**: no other command runs while it executes, so it can read, decide and write without race conditions or WATCH and trying again.

Rules that matter:

- pass every key the script touches in `KEYS` and never build key names inside it; Redis Cluster (several servers sharing the data, an Expert lesson) uses them to send the script to the right server, and all the keys must live on the same one,
- keep scripts short: a long-running script holds up the whole server (`busy-reply-threshold`, default 5 seconds, after which only `SCRIPT KILL` or `SHUTDOWN NOSAVE` are accepted),
- a script should give the same result for the same inputs, so avoid randomness and the current time.

`SCRIPT LOAD` stores a script on the server and returns its id (a SHA1 fingerprint of its text); `EVALSHA id ...` runs it without resending the text. Client libraries handle the `NOSCRIPT` reply (script not stored yet) for you.

**Redis Functions** (7.0+) are the managed successor: `FUNCTION LOAD` registers a named set of functions that is saved with the data and copied to replicas, and `FCALL name numkeys ...` calls one. Prefer functions for logic that is a permanent part of your application.

A classic use is a safe lock release: delete the lock only if it still holds your own value, which a plain `GET` then `DEL` from the client can't do atomically.
concepts.code:
# release a lock only if we still own it (atomic compare-and-delete)
redis-cli SET lock:report tok-123 NX EX 30            # OK
redis-cli EVAL "if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end" 1 lock:report tok-999
# (integer) 0   wrong token, lock kept
redis-cli EVAL "if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end" 1 lock:report tok-123
# (integer) 1   released

# the same as a named Redis Function
redis-cli FUNCTION LOAD "#!lua name=locks
redis.register_function('unlock', function(keys, args)
  if redis.call('GET', keys[1]) == args[1] then return redis.call('DEL', keys[1]) end
  return 0 end)"                                       # "locks"
redis-cli FCALL unlock 1 lock:report tok-123          # (integer) 0  already gone
takeaways: Scripts run atomically on the server: read, decide, write in one step
Pass all keys via KEYS so Redis Cluster knows where to run the script
Long scripts block everyone; keep them fast
Functions (7.0+) are named scripts, saved with the data and copied to replicas called with FCALL
pitfalls: Building key names inside a script from ARGV: it breaks on Redis Cluster and hides keys from Redis.

quiz.q: Why can't a client safely release a lock with GET followed by DEL when the value matches?
options: The lock may expire and be taken by another client between the GET and the DEL
GET is not allowed on lock keys
quiz.explain: The two commands aren't atomic, so another owner's lock could be deleted; a script does both atomically.

concepts.name: Persistence: RDB and AOF
concepts.summary: Choose between RDB snapshots and the append-only file, and know how much data a crash can cost you.
concepts.why: Whether Redis can be trusted to keep your data, or only to cache it, depends entirely on how it saves to disk.
concepts.body:
Redis keeps data in memory, which is emptied when the server stops or crashes. To survive that it can save to disk (**persistence**) in two ways, usable together.

**RDB snapshots** write a compact copy of all the data as it was at one moment (a **snapshot**, saved as `dump.rdb`) at intervals, configured with `save <seconds> <changes>` rules or started with `BGSAVE`. Redis makes a copy of its own running program to do it (a **fork**): the copy writes the file while the original keeps serving clients.

The fork doesn't double memory straight away: both copies share the same memory, and a piece is only duplicated when one of them changes it (**copy-on-write**). RDB files are great for backups and fast restarts, but a crash loses everything since the last snapshot, possibly minutes of writes.

**AOF (append-only file)** records every write command in a file, like a diary. `appendfsync` controls how often Redis forces that file onto the disk (an **fsync**; until then the newest writes may exist only in memory):

- `always`: fsync after every write, safest and slowest,
- `everysec` (recommended default): fsync once per second, losing at most about a second of writes,
- `no`: let the **operating system** (the computer's base software, such as Linux) decide.

The AOF keeps growing, so Redis regularly **rewrites** it in the background into the shortest list of commands that rebuilds the same data. Since 7.0 the AOF is a set of files (a base file, files of recent changes, and an index file listing them) in `appenddirname`.

Typical setups: a pure cache can turn persistence off; a store whose data matters uses AOF `everysec`, often with RDB as well for backups. On restart with AOF enabled, Redis loads the AOF because it is more complete.

Watch out for the fork: with lots of data and heavy writes, copy-on-write can temporarily double memory use, so leave spare memory. If the server runs short, the operating system starts moving memory out to disk (swapping) and everything slows to a crawl.
concepts.code:
# redis.conf (or CONFIG SET at runtime)
save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000     # RDB: snapshot if 1 change/1h, 100/5min, 10000/1min
appendonly yes                   # enable AOF
appendfsync everysec             # lose at most ~1 s of writes
appenddirname "appendonlydir"
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100  # rewrite when AOF doubles
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb

# operations from the shell
redis-cli BGSAVE                 # Background saving started
redis-cli LASTSAVE               # (integer) 1760700000  unix time of last save
redis-cli INFO persistence | grep -E 'rdb_last_bgsave_status|aof_enabled'   # grep keeps matching lines
# rdb_last_bgsave_status:ok
# aof_enabled:1
takeaways: RDB: periodic snapshots written by a fork; compact, may lose minutes
AOF: records every write; everysec loses at most about one second
Both can be enabled; AOF is used for recovery when present
Forking can briefly double memory under heavy writes
pitfalls: Treating Redis with the default snapshot-only settings as a database that never loses data.

quiz.q: With appendonly yes and appendfsync everysec, how much acknowledged data can a power loss destroy?
options: Everything since the last RDB snapshot
quiz.explain: The AOF is fsynced once per second, so roughly the last second may be lost.

concepts.name: Memory limits and eviction
concepts.summary: Cap memory with maxmemory, pick an eviction policy, and find what is using memory.
concepts.why: When Redis runs out of RAM it either deletes data or refuses writes; you must choose which.
concepts.body:
`maxmemory` sets the memory limit (for example `4gb`). When it is reached, `maxmemory-policy`, the **eviction policy**, decides what happens on a write. Removing keys to make room is called **eviction**.

- `noeviction` (default): writes that need more memory fail with an out-of-memory (OOM) error, reads still work; right for data you can't lose,
- `allkeys-lru` / `allkeys-lfu`: evict the **least recently used** (LRU) or **least frequently used** (LFU) keys anywhere; right for caches,
- `volatile-lru`, `volatile-lfu`, `volatile-ttl`, `volatile-random`: only evict keys that have an expiry, so you can mix permanent keys and cache keys,
- `allkeys-random`.

LRU and LFU are approximate: Redis checks a small random sample of keys (`maxmemory-samples`, default 5) instead of tracking the exact order, which is cheap and close enough. LFU suits data where a few keys are always popular.

Leave spare RAM beyond `maxmemory`. Redis also needs memory for the gaps left between stored values (fragmentation), for data waiting to be sent to clients and replicas, and for forks.

Finding what uses memory:

- `INFO memory` shows `used_memory`, `used_memory_rss` and `mem_fragmentation_ratio`,
- `MEMORY USAGE key` reports bytes for one key, `MEMORY DOCTOR` gives advice,
- `redis-cli --bigkeys` and `--memkeys` sample the keys to find the largest.

Keep values small, prefer hashes for many small fields, set TTLs on cache keys, and avoid **big keys** (huge lists, sets or hashes), which also make the server pause when they are deleted or moved.
concepts.code:
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory 100mb                # OK
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu   # OK
redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy
# 1) "maxmemory-policy"  2) "allkeys-lfu"

redis-cli SET greeting "hello"                      # OK
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE greeting
# (integer) 56   bytes, including Redis's own bookkeeping (varies)
redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E '^(used_memory_human|maxmemory_human|mem_fragmentation_ratio)'
# grep keeps only those lines:
# used_memory_human:2.42M        (varies)
# maxmemory_human:100.00M
# mem_fragmentation_ratio:1.20    (varies)
redis-cli --bigkeys                                 # scans and reports the biggest keys
takeaways: maxmemory + maxmemory-policy decide what happens when RAM is full
noeviction (default) fails writes; allkeys-lru/lfu suits caches
volatile-* policies evict only keys with a TTL
Use INFO memory, MEMORY USAGE and --bigkeys to find what uses memory
pitfalls: Running a cache with the default noeviction policy and getting out-of-memory errors on writes once it fills.

quiz.q: Redis holds both permanent configuration keys (no TTL) and cache keys (with TTL). Which policy evicts only cache keys?
quiz.explain: volatile-* policies only consider keys that have an expiry set.

concepts.name: Replication and Sentinel
concepts.summary: Copy a primary to replicas without waiting for them, and use Sentinel to switch to a replica automatically when the primary fails.
concepts.why: Keeping Redis running through failures (high availability) means understanding how its copies can fall behind and what can be lost.
concepts.body:
A **replica** is a second Redis server that keeps a copy of another server's data; the server it copies is the **primary**. A replica connects with `REPLICAOF host port`. First it does a full sync: the primary forks to write an RDB snapshot and sends it over, followed by the writes that arrived meanwhile. After that the replica receives every write command as it happens.

After a short disconnect a replica catches up with a **partial resync**, replaying recent writes the primary keeps in a fixed-size **replication backlog** (`repl-backlog-size`). If it has missed more than that, it needs a new full sync.

Replication is **asynchronous**: the primary confirms a write to the client before the replicas have it. If the primary dies, the last writes may be lost when a replica takes over. `WAIT numreplicas timeout` waits until that many replicas have the previous writes, narrowing (not closing) the gap. `min-replicas-to-write` makes a primary refuse writes when too few replicas are connected, which limits the damage when the network splits and the primary is cut off from the rest.

Replicas are read-only by default and can serve reads, which may be slightly out of date.

**Redis Sentinel** switches to a replica automatically when the primary fails (**failover**), for setups without Redis Cluster. Run at least three Sentinel programs on separate machines. They watch the primary; when enough of them agree it is down (a **quorum**, set in their configuration), one Sentinel is chosen to run the switch: it promotes the best replica, points the other replicas at it and announces the new address. Clients ask Sentinel for the current primary (`SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name mymaster`) instead of hard-coding it.

**Split brain** is the classic hazard: an old primary cut off from the others keeps accepting writes, which are thrown away when it rejoins as a replica.
concepts.code:
# on the replica
redis-cli -p 6380 REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6379          # OK
redis-cli -p 6380 INFO replication | grep -E 'role|master_link_status'
# role:slave
# master_link_status:up

# on the primary: wait until 1 replica has the previous writes (max 100 ms)
redis-cli SET balance:ana 100                        # OK
redis-cli WAIT 1 100                                 # (integer) 1

# sentinel.conf (one of three Sentinels)
# sentinel monitor mymaster 10.0.0.1 6379 2          # quorum 2
# sentinel down-after-milliseconds mymaster 5000
# sentinel failover-timeout mymaster 60000
redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name mymaster
# 1) "10.0.0.1"  2) "6379"
takeaways: Replicas do a full sync, then follow every write; the backlog allows a partial resync
Replication is asynchronous: confirmed writes can be lost on failover
WAIT and min-replicas-to-write narrow the loss window
Sentinel (3 or more) detects failure by quorum and promotes a replica
pitfalls: Running a single Sentinel, which is itself a single point of failure and can't form a quorum.

quiz.q: A client gets OK for a write, then the primary crashes before replicating it and a replica is promoted. What happens to the write?
options: It is replayed from the client's buffer
Sentinel copies it from the dead primary
quiz.explain: Asynchronous replication means acknowledged but unreplicated writes can be lost.

concepts.name: Redis Cluster and hash slots
concepts.summary: Spread data over several servers using 16384 hash slots, use hash tags for multi-key commands, and follow MOVED and ASK replies.
concepts.why: When one server's memory or processor isn't enough, Redis Cluster spreads the data over several, but it changes how you design keys.
concepts.body:
**Redis Cluster** splits the data across several primaries, each with its own replicas; splitting data over machines like this is **sharding**. Every key belongs to one of **16384 hash slots**: its slot is `CRC16(key) mod 16384`, a fixed calculation that turns the key name into a number. Each primary owns a set of slots.

There is no middleman server: clients know about the cluster, keep a copy of the slot map, and send each command straight to the right server. If a client asks the wrong one, it gets `-MOVED slot host:port` (update your map) or, while a slot is being moved, `-ASK` (try the other server once). Good client libraries handle both.

Commands that use several keys (`MGET`, `SINTER`, transactions, Lua scripts) only work when all the keys are in the **same slot**; otherwise you get `CROSSSLOT`. **Hash tags** solve this: only the part inside the first `{...}` is used to pick the slot, so `{user:42}:profile` and `{user:42}:cart` share one. Put tags around the thing your operations group by, not a constant, or one slot gets all the traffic.

Other differences from a single server:

- only database 0 exists,
- failover is built in: the primaries vote to promote a replica of a failed primary,
- slots can be moved between servers while the cluster runs (`redis-cli --cluster reshard`),
- `cluster-require-full-coverage` decides whether the cluster stops when some slots have no working server.

As with Sentinel, cluster replication is asynchronous, so the same window for losing writes applies.
concepts.code:
redis-cli --cluster create 10.0.0.1:6379 10.0.0.2:6379 10.0.0.3:6379 \
  10.0.0.4:6379 10.0.0.5:6379 10.0.0.6:6379 --cluster-replicas 1

redis-cli -c -h 10.0.0.1 CLUSTER KEYSLOT user:42          # (integer) 6929 (example)
redis-cli -c -h 10.0.0.1 CLUSTER KEYSLOT '{user:42}:cart'  # same slot as {user:42}:profile
redis-cli -c -h 10.0.0.1 MSET a 1 b 2
# (error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot
redis-cli -c -h 10.0.0.1 MSET '{user:42}:a' 1 '{user:42}:b' 2   # OK
redis-cli -h 10.0.0.1 GET some-key-on-another-node
# (error) MOVED 12182 10.0.0.3:6379   (-c makes redis-cli follow it)
redis-cli -h 10.0.0.1 CLUSTER SHARDS        # slot ranges, primaries and replicas
takeaways: 16384 slots; slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384; each primary owns some slots
Clients follow MOVED/ASK replies and keep a copy of the slot map
Multi-key operations need one slot: use {hash tags}
Only database 0; replication is still asynchronous
pitfalls: Using one constant hash tag like {app} for every key: all data lands in one slot on one node.

quiz.q: Which pair of keys can be used together in one MGET on a Redis Cluster?
quiz.explain: With identical hash tags both keys hash to the same slot.

concepts.name: Event loop, encodings and latency
concepts.summary: Understand Redis's single main thread, its I/O threads, compact memory formats and what causes sudden slowdowns.
concepts.why: Diagnosing a slow Redis means knowing what holds up its main thread and how data is laid out in memory.
concepts.body:
A **thread** is one line of work inside a running program. Redis runs every command on one **main thread**, driven by an **event loop**: it keeps asking the operating system which client connections have something to read or send (epoll/kqueue) and handles them one at a time. That's why commands are atomic and why Redis needs no locks, but also why one slow command delays every client.

Since Redis 6, optional **I/O threads** (`io-threads`; I/O means input/output, here reading from and writing to the network) can read incoming commands and send replies side by side, and Redis 8 improved this a lot. The commands themselves still run one at a time. Other background threads free memory for `UNLINK`, force the AOF to disk and close files.

Common causes of slowdowns:

- commands whose cost grows with size, on big keys: `KEYS`, `HGETALL`/`SMEMBERS`/`LRANGE 0 -1` on huge collections, `DEL` of a big key (use `UNLINK` and the lazyfree options),
- slow Lua scripts,
- the fork for an RDB save or AOF rewrite on a server with lots of data, made worse by the Linux setting "transparent huge pages", which makes copy-on-write copy much bigger pieces (turn it off),
- swapping, and `appendfsync always` on slow disks.

Tools: `SLOWLOG GET` lists commands slower than `slowlog-log-slower-than` (microseconds), `LATENCY DOCTOR` and `redis-cli --latency` measure delays, and `INFO commandstats` shows totals per command.

**Encodings**: Redis stores small collections in compact layouts that pack items one after another. Hashes, sorted sets and lists use **listpack** while small, sets of whole numbers use **intset**, and they switch to bigger, faster structures (hash tables, skiplists, quicklists) once they pass thresholds like `hash-max-listpack-entries` (128 fields) or a value passes `hash-max-listpack-value` (64 bytes). `OBJECT ENCODING key` shows the current one. Keeping collections under the thresholds can cut memory several-fold.
concepts.code:
redis-cli HSET small f1 v1                  # (integer) 1
redis-cli OBJECT ENCODING small             # "listpack"
redis-cli SADD ids 1 2 3                    # (integer) 3
redis-cli OBJECT ENCODING ids               # "intset"
redis-cli HSET small f2 "this value is deliberately longer than sixty-four bytes, so the format changes"
redis-cli OBJECT ENCODING small             # "hashtable"
redis-cli ZADD z 1 a                        # (integer) 1
redis-cli OBJECT ENCODING z                 # "listpack" (skiplist when large)

redis-cli CONFIG SET slowlog-log-slower-than 10000   # log commands > 10 ms
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 5                     # id, timestamp, microseconds, command
redis-cli INFO commandstats | head -3       # cmdstat_hset:calls=...,usec_per_call=...
takeaways: One main thread executes all commands; I/O threads only help with networking
Big keys, O(N) commands, slow scripts and forks cause latency spikes
SLOWLOG, LATENCY DOCTOR and commandstats locate them
Small collections use compact listpack/intset formats that save lots of memory
pitfalls: Adding io-threads to fix a slow command that is busy calculating: commands still run one at a time.

quiz.q: A single DEL on a 50-million-member set freezes Redis for seconds. What is the better command?
quiz.explain: UNLINK removes the key immediately and frees memory in a background thread.
